title: Help Your Children Understand AI's Place https://rootedministry.com/help-your-children-understand-ais-place-three-foundational-truths-for-ai-use/
author: Luke Paiva
summary: Luke Paiva, a high school Bible teacher and father of four, writes for Christian parents about how AI is changing the classroom and what children need to understand about it. He reports that students type a question, read the AI summary, and give up if the answer is not there, and that they produce correct-sounding answers without engaging the questions they are meant to wrestle with. His concern is less AI itself than its marketing as an authority instead of a collector of possibilities. He offers three foundational truths: AI compiles what is on the internet, so children must judge its output critically; wisdom cannot be found everywhere on the internet and comes through Scripture, prayer, and community; and creativity and critical thinking weaken when unused. He rejects banning AI as futile and urges teaching students to use it as an assistant that sharpens thinking, never as something that carries the full load.
points: Paiva's classroom observation is that students give up when the AI summary lacks the answer and cannot relate correct-sounding responses to the ideas they were asked to wrestle with.
He locates the danger in AI's marketing as an authority rather than a collector of possibilities, which invites submission to the tool.
His first truth is that AI compiles good and bad ideas from the internet, so children must be taught to evaluate its output rather than trust an algorithm.
His second truth is that moral and spiritual wisdom is not all found online and requires people who cultivate virtue through prayer, fellowship, and Scripture.
He argues against banning AI and for teaching students to use it as an assistant, since creativity and critical thinking atrophy when the work of thinking is outsourced.
quotes: However, creations make terrible masters, and any tool can be destructive if misused. The greatest danger of AI is if our children—or we—sacrifice our minds to the simplicity and ease of our own creation.
They type in a search question and read the AI summary. If what they were looking for isn’t there, they give up.
It is a foreign concept to many students to read through multiple sources, evaluate the information, or re-evaluate the questions they’re searching for.
When asked to clarify their answers and relate them to the ideas, they do not understand. They have abandoned critical thinking for easy access to information provided by a tool.
Companies advertised AI as an authority rather than a collector of possibilities. I have witnessed adults and students alike fall victim to this trap.
That means children need to be tough to think critically about whether or not the AI response is good.
It is tempting to let something take over the work of thinking and creating, because it is work. But it is good work—necessary work.
Banning its use is futile. We should teach students how to use AI properly, harnessing it as a tool that can sharpen our critical thinking and fuel our creativity.
